Agats (port locode IDAGA) is a port town and the administrative center of Asmat Regency (South Papua, Indonesia). The town has a population of around 1500. It is located near the Aswetsj River's estuary.

As a cruise port, Agats is visited by smaller ships and mega-yachts operated by luxury travel brands, like Seabourn.

Agats was established in the early 20th century (1938) as a Dutch outpost. It became the Agats District's capital and an administrative seat in November 2002, when the Asmat Regency (kabupaten) was formed by splitting off from the Merauke Regency. The Agats District consists of 12 villages (kampung).

The Asmat Regency (1969-formed) is bounded by the Arafura Sea (to the southwest), the Mappi Regency (to the southeast and east), the Highland Papua Province (to the north), and the Central Papua Province (to the northwest). It became part of the South Papua Province in 2022. 

Asmat Regency's total population is around 120,000. The Asmat region is renowned for its cultural diversity, including wood carving practices and traditional ceremonies. Today, the Asmat Regency comprises 25 districts and 4 offshore islands.

Agats is a remote expedition-style cruise call in South Papua and the gateway to the Asmat cultural region. The town itself is unusual: much of it stands above tidal swamp on raised wooden or concrete walkways, with electric motorcycles rather than conventional road traffic. Central Agats can be explored on foot, but the river journeys and village visits that are the main reason for calling here are best handled through the ship or an organized local guide.

At a Glance

  • Best approach: Organized excursion recommended for Asmat village and river experiences; central Agats can be explored independently if the ship permits free time ashore.
  • Cruise access: Expedition ships generally anchor near Agats and use Zodiacs or other ship boats rather than placing passengers at a conventional cruise terminal.
  • Walkability: Good within town, but the raised boardwalks can be uneven, narrow or slippery.
  • Main sights: Museum of Asmat Culture and Progress, Holy Cross Cathedral, the raised town, local market and nearby Syuru community.
  • Beyond town: Travel is primarily by river. Independent longboat trips are not a good choice during a short cruise call.

Getting Ashore and Around

Agats has local ferry and sea-port facilities, but visiting cruise ships normally operate differently. Published expedition itineraries describe ships entering the shallow Flamingo River area when conditions allow, anchoring near Agats and transferring passengers by Zodiac or ship boat. Tide and river conditions can affect the exact landing point and timetable, so follow the arrangements announced onboard rather than assuming passengers will use the town ferry pier.

Once ashore, most central sights can be reached on foot. Agats has no normal road network for cars; its streets are largely raised wooden or concrete walkways over swampy ground. Electric motorcycles are the principal local vehicle, and motorcycle taxis operate locally, but walking is normally more practical for cruise visitors staying in the center.

There is no useful tourist public-transport network for reaching the surrounding Asmat communities. Villages are connected mainly by rivers and waterways, making ship-operated or locally guided boat trips the sensible option.

Best Ways to Spend Your Time

Explore Agats and the Asmat Museum

Allow about 2–3 hours. Walking through Agats is an attraction in itself, with homes, shops, government buildings and public spaces raised above the tidal wetlands. The most important stop is the Museum of Asmat Culture and Progress, whose collection includes carvings, shields, drums, ceremonial objects and other material from communities across the Asmat region.

The museum is particularly worthwhile before or after a village visit because it provides context for Asmat carving, ceremonies and traditional life. It publishes daytime opening Monday through Saturday, while Sunday and holiday closure is stated; published closing times vary, so cruise visitors should confirm access with expedition staff.

Join an Asmat Village and Cultural Visit

Usually a half-day expedition activity. This is generally the most significant experience of an Agats call and is best done with the cruise line or an experienced local operator. Expedition programs commonly use Zodiacs or motorboats to travel through the Asewet River delta and surrounding waterways before visiting an Asmat community.

Depending on arrangements, visits may include traditional canoes, carving, a communal Jew house, music or ceremonial performances. These are community visits rather than attractions that passengers should attempt to reach independently. River conditions, tides and local arrangements determine what is possible on a particular day.

Walk to Syuru

Allow about 1.5–2 hours from central Agats and back. Syuru lies immediately beside Agats and is one of the nearest Asmat communities accessible via the raised walkway network. Local sources describe it as roughly a 10-minute walk from the central town area. The community is associated with a traditional Jew communal house and is also used as a venue during Asmat cultural events.

This is more practical than trying to arrange an independent boat to a distant village, but visitors should treat Syuru as a living community rather than an open-air attraction. A local guide is preferable, especially if entering community buildings or photographing residents.

River and Mangrove Exploration

Allow 2–4 hours depending on the ship's program. Agats is surrounded by broad muddy rivers, tidal channels, mangroves and swamp forest rather than conventional beaches. Zodiac or small-boat exploration can therefore be more rewarding than remaining entirely in town, with opportunities to observe the landscape and river-based way of life.

This should normally be booked or arranged through the expedition team. Tide levels and rapidly changing weather can influence navigation, and independent boat arrangements introduce unnecessary return-to-ship risk.

Self-Guided Agats Walking Tour

Central Agats Cultural Walk

Approximate distance: 3–5 km (1.9–3.1 mi), depending on the ship's landing point and whether Syuru is included.
Pure walking time: about 50–80 minutes.
Recommended total time: 2.5–3.5 hours with museum and sightseeing stops.
Difficulty: Easy to moderate. The route is essentially flat, but raised wooden walkways can be uneven, wet and slippery.

  1. Cruise landing point: Begin wherever the expedition team brings passengers ashore. Confirm the required final Zodiac or tender departure before leaving the landing area.
  2. Agats boardwalks: Walk through the central raised streets to see how the town functions above tidal swamp. Watch for quietly approaching electric motorcycles.
  3. Local market: Make a short stop to see everyday trading and produce from the surrounding river communities.
  4. Holy Cross Cathedral: Visit the cathedral area, long associated with the Catholic Diocese of Agats and Asmat cultural preservation. Construction of a new cathedral building was still underway in mid-2026, so access and appearance may vary.
  5. Museum of Asmat Culture and Progress: Allow at least 45–60 minutes for the collection of Asmat carvings and cultural objects.
  6. Optional Syuru extension: Continue along the walkway network into nearby Syuru if time and local arrangements permit, then return directly toward central Agats.
  7. Return to the landing: Be back well before the ship's stated final boat time; expedition operations may change with tides or weather.

Passengers with limited mobility should be cautious. Even though there are no significant hills, some sections may involve narrow walkways, irregular boards, steps and surfaces that become slick after rain.

Practical Tips

  • Do not expect a conventional beach day. Agats is a tidal river and mangrove destination.
  • Wear shoes with good grip rather than sandals with smooth soles; wet boardwalks can be slippery.
  • Carry rain protection, drinking water, sun protection and insect repellent. Conditions are typically hot and humid.
  • Ask before photographing residents, ceremonies or the interior of community buildings.
  • For carvings or handicrafts, buying directly from recognized local artisans can support the community; follow any guidance from expedition staff concerning transport or customs restrictions.
  • Avoid arranging an independent long-distance river trip during a cruise call. Travel times are variable and there are few backup transport options.
  • For Zodiac operations, always work backward from the ship's final boat time rather than its scheduled departure time and keep a generous return margin.
